entities.name: PMID:27491601
observations: Mina et al., JACC Cardiovascular Interventions, 2016; meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (27,491 ACS patients) with outcomes stratified by vascular access and anticoagulation.

Within femoral-access patients, bivalirudin versus heparin reduced major bleeding (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.46–0.60; p<0.001); within radial-access patients, estimate was not significant (OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.45–1.26; p=0.28).

Within heparin-treated patients, radial versus femoral access reduced major bleeding (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43–0.77; p<0.001); within bivalirudin-treated patients, estimate was not significant (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.65–1.41; p=0.83).

No MACE or all-cause mortality differences between anticoagulants regardless of access site. Authors concluded combined bivalirudin plus radial access has no additional benefit over either strategy separately. Abstract does not report a formal treatment-interaction test or direct randomized assignment to the combined versus alternative strategies.

entities.name: No additive bleeding benefit
observations: In an eight-trial ACS meta-analysis (27,491 patients), neither bivalirudin within radial procedures nor radial access within bivalirudin procedures significantly reduced major bleeding; estimates were OR 0.75 (95% CI 0.45–1.26) and OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.65–1.41), respectively.

The evidence supports no demonstrated additive advantage of combining bivalirudin with radial access; stratified trial subgroup comparisons are not equivalent to a dedicated randomized comparison of the combined strategy.
